title: Allowing Makers to Adopt Certain Markings for National Firearms Act Firearms
pass_4_primary_concern: The cost-benefit and traceability case is plausible but only partly evidenced, especially on how often the adopted-markings approach affects real-world tracing and maker behavior.
pass_5_high_stakes_domain_reason: The proposal concerns National Firearms Act firearms, traceability, and law-enforcement recovery of regulated weapons.
pass_5_concise_why: The rule is mostly coherent but still under-evidenced on the central tracing premise and on the size of the indirect economic spillovers.
pass_5_most_important_consequence: If the traceability premise is overstated, the final rule could reduce physical redundancy without showing that the registry and original marks fully substitute for maker marks.

pass_5_flaws.explanation: The rule does not substitute private authority for agency authority; ATF itself proposes the change.
The proposal appears to implement the marking statute rather than invert it.
The notice does not shift accountability away from ATF or the regulated maker in a structurally unusual way.
The rule keeps a federal registry and existing marking baseline; it does not rely purely on self-policing.
The proposal does not obviously reorder constraints so that the public bears the loss before review.
The rule still has a traceability premise, but this record does not justify treating the evidence gap as material.
The remedy/rationale fit is adequate enough that this axis should not carry weight on its own.
The proposal is implementable on its face and does not rely on impossible operational changes.
The rule does not depend on a nonexistent technical interface or an opaque external system.
The proposal discusses traceability and burden, not a vaguely defined threat model.
The indirect small-entity effect is real but not strong enough here to score as a material loss of emphasis.
The rule does not create an obvious new abuse surface aimed at particular individuals or groups.
The remaining safeguard question is not a standalone structural flaw in this docket.
The spillover is too small and too speculative to count as a material externality on this pass.
The rule does not create a new suspicion-based gatekeeping system.
The NFRTR and underlying manufacturer marks remain part of the accountability substrate.
This is a proposal, not a completed operative change, so there is no finalized harm-before-review structure yet.
The rule does not create a new procedural choke point or permit gate.
The consequences are relatively clear: reduced marking burden and possible reduced gunsmith work.
The exception is textually specific and not obviously an ambiguity-driven gatekeeping device.
The rule remains coherent enough that this axis should not be counted as a material defect.
